study_type.claude: Case study (description of the process of creating benchmark components)
study_type.nlm: Mixed methods (case study, literature review, cognitive testing, pilot, RCT, surveys)
study_type.note: Claude: Case study; NotebookLM: Mixed methods. The paper calls itself a case study (CHI EA case-study track) describing instrument development; the RCT results are published elsewhere ([20], arXiv).

research_method.claude: Case study of a five-step benchmark-creation process: survey question drafting, literature review of AI-attitude questions, cognitive testing (9 and 8 engineers), pilot (8 sessions), between-subject RCT design
research_method.nlm: Case study, literature review, cognitive testing (2 rounds, 17 engineers), pilot testing (8 iterations), RCT protocol, surveys
research_method.value: Description of a five-step process to build DX benchmark components for genAI coding features: metric selection and survey drafting, literature review of AI-attitude questions, two rounds of cognitive (think-aloud) testing (9 and 8 Google engineers), 8 pilot sessions of an enterprise-grade C++ task, and a between-subject RCT protocol (with vs. without AI; velocity results reported in a separate paper)
research_method.note: Same design described by both; only the study_type label differs.

context.claude: Industry; Google, AI for code features in internal IDE, enterprise-grade C++ task; 9 + 8 engineers in cognitive testing, 8 pilot sessions
context.nlm: Industry; Google, backend C++ development, internal IDE tools; 17 engineers in cognitive testing, 8 C++ developers in pilot
context.value: industry; Google, AI-for-code features in internal IDE, enterprise-grade C++ task; 17 software engineers in cognitive testing (9 + 8) and 8 pilot sessions with C++ developers
context.note: Final RCT sample not reported in this paper.

space_applied.note: Metrics selected from Google's internal DX metrics framework, 'a variant of the SPACE framework'. Claude: SPACE applied (via the variant); NotebookLM: SPACE referenced, internal framework applied.

ai_discussed.note: Benchmarking the DX and velocity impact of genAI coding features.

remote_covid.note: Work mode not specified by either (self-administered, asynchronous activities; 'globally-distributed' engineers only motivates language testing).

cat_productivity.note: Velocity defined as time to complete an enterprise-grade task (logged), plus perceived productivity items.

cat_quality.note: Perceived code quality (quality of code suggestion; long-term impact on the code base), survey-based.

cat_satisfaction.note: Overall satisfaction with AI feature (sentiment metrics).

cat_activity.note: Claude labels self-reported AI usage frequency 'Activity'; NotebookLM labels goal importance 'Activity / Context'; neither is repository activity.

cat_delivery.note: NotebookLM labels time on task 'Productivity / Delivery'; it is task completion time (Productivity).

cat_devex.note: 'Developer experience (DX)' is used generically; both use 'DevEx' as a loose label; the Noda/Storey/Forsgren framework is not used.

cat_survey.note: Demographics/attitude questionnaires, post-task and feature surveys (sentiment metrics).

evidence.quote: The first round of cognitive testing was focused on the task and feature questions, and was conducted with 9 full-time software engineers at Google.
The second round of cognitive testing was conducted with 8 full-time software engineers at Google, and focused on demographic, current use of AI, and AI attitudes questions.
We continued recruiting and iterating until the task was completed in under 1.5 hours and without researcher intervention three times in a row, which took eight sessions in total.
A schematic overview of our between-subject human experimental design and its components can be found in Figure 1.

The main aim of this project was to support our team with high-quality data to evaluate the user experience of our AI for code features, including an estimate of the impact of AI-enhanced coding tools on developer velocity (see [20]).
We defined velocity as the time taken to complete an enterprise-grade engineering task, with or without AI, from the branching of code all the way through to testing and building the code.
